transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-09
Time: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Head of ML, Equinox), Tom Reynolds (Platform Eng), Sara Lee (Security)

Auto-generated summary (may be partial):
- Deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy, hit-rate modeling, cache key design, multi-tenant safety and access controls, TTLs and invalidation, interplay with KV cache and batching, quantization effects, and on-prem/VPC considerations.
- Agreed next steps: share docs, run 1-week pilot with representative prompt set, schedule on-prem benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I see Priya, Tom, Sara, thanks for making time. We'll run through prefix caching patterns, hit rates, multi-tenant safety, and then where that lives in Redwood's runtime. Marco and I will lead.
[00:18] Priya: thanks Lena. quick context, we're seeing a lot of repeated system prompts and user prompt templates across our product - want to understand how to cache prefixes safely without leaking across tenants and how that affects latency under our 50ms per-token SLO target.
[00:34] Marco: got it. real quick, when we say prefix caching here we're talking about storing KV cache state for repeated prompt prefixes - so on a local serving node we rehydrate the KV cache instead of recomputing attention for the prefix. sometimes in notes people call it prefix-kw cache or KV cash, it's the same idea.
[00:50] Tom: small note - our infra is hybrid, most traffic goes through VPC peering to Redwood Private but we may also use hosted for burst. security is big for us, Sara will ask questions there.
[01:05] Sara: yeah we need to see audit logs and KMS integration, and we can't have any cross-tenant cache contamination. also TTLs need to be explicit, and ability to evict or scope caches to an org id.
[01:20] Marco: totally. high-level pattern we recommend: cache keys = hash(prefix_text + model_id + model_version + tenant_id + prompt_params). include tenant_id as a namespace - that buys multi-tenant separation. key also includes quantization and execution profile tags (eg q4_0 / int8) because those change the KV layout.
[01:44] Priya: wait, model_version and quantization? if we change quantization will previously cached prefixes be invalid?
[01:50] Lena: yes, if quantization or low-level kernel selection changes the representational format of the KV cache you must invalidate or version the cache. that's why we include quantization tag in the key. Marco, you had hit-rate numbers?
[02:02] Marco: right, we looked at Equinox's sample prompts you sent - with stable system prompts and ~20 templated user prompts we estimate prefix reuse hit rates of ~45-60% for cold-start sessions after a short training period. hit-rate is sensitive to how you canonicalize prompts - whitespace, user metadata, ordering of JSON keys, we need normalization.
[02:26] Tom: normalization pipeline - ok. what about TTLs? how long do prefixes live?
[02:31] Marco: depends on traffic patterns. typical strategy: short TTLs for high-churn dynamic prompts (30-300s), longer TTLs for stable system prompts (hours). you can make TTLs adaptive using LRU + access frequency, and also add explicit invalidation hooks when a model or system prompt changes.
[02:49] Priya: can you illustrate the savings? numbers help when we present this internally.
[02:54] Marco: sure. on a 2k token prefix with 8 attention layers on a 70B model, rehydrating KV cache reduces per-token latency by ~30-50% versus re-evaluating prefix; throughput increases similarly because less compute per request. we measured per-token CPU/GPU cycles down by about 40% in our benchmarks. I'll share the benchmark sheet but rough numbers are latency cut from 14ms/token to ~8-10ms/token for the prefix portion.
[03:20] Tom: does batching interact with this? we rely on batching to get throughput.
[03:24] Marco: yes, interplay is important. two modes: pre-batch rehydrate then batch decode, or batch with on-the-fly KV merge. rehydrating per-request then batching decode is simpler and avoids complex merging, but increases memory. continuous batching with shared prefix levels is more efficient but requires runtime support to ensure compatible cache shapes and same seq-len alignment. Redwood runtime supports both patterns; depends on your SLOs.
[03:52] Sara: memory isolation question - if many tenants have cached prefixes, do caches accumulate on the same node and risk OOM?
[03:58] Marco: we expose per-tenant quotas and eviction policies. in Dedicated/Private deployments you can set reserved cache memory per tenant or route tenants to separate GPU pools. we also have soft quotas + hard eviction and LRU. for on-prem you'll control the node sizes and we provide operators with dashboards to evict or pin entries.
[04:18] Priya: are there attacks where one tenant could craft prefixes that cause another's cache to evict? like eviction churn DOS?
[04:27] Marco: good question. multi-tenant safety patterns: namespace keys (tenant_id in key) prevents direct reads of another tenant's cache. eviction DOS can happen if you put all tenants on same eviction pool - mitigation: per-tenant reservation slices or admission controls, and cost-aware eviction where larger prefix entries have higher eviction cost. we recommend using dedicated pools for high-value tenants.
[04:52] Tom: what about cache integrity - could a compromised worker restore bad KV states?
[04:56] Lena: in Private we integrate with KMS and we sign cache metadata; for hosted we isolate keys per-tenant and maintain strict ACLs. we log rehydrate events for audit. Sara, we can show sample audit entries.
[05:08] Sara: yes please, and also need SOC2 artifacts.
[05:12] Marco: back to cache keys - don't store PII in key material; hash salted prefixes. and include a version field so you can roll forward/back quickly. we also instrument hit/miss and per-key sizes - Equinox's prompt histogram will help pick sensible TTLs.
[05:31] Priya: quantization - does Q4_0 vs int8 change the cache size?
[05:35] Marco: yes Q4_0 has different packed layout; cached KV size differs and rehydration code path differs, that's why we include quant tag in key. in practice quantization reduces memory footprint but may increase CPU deserialization latency depending on kernel. we'll show microbenchmarks.
[05:51] Tom: do you support dynamic quantization toggles per-request? we sometimes run mixed workloads.
[05:57] Marco: you can route by model_variant field in key; mixed workloads okay but keep in mind that incompatible variants can't share entries. if you have hybrid workloads it's better to maintain separate cache namespaces or use on-the-fly conversion (costly).
[06:12] Priya: can you walk through an example key and lifecycle?
[06:15] Marco: example key -> sha256(tenant_id || '::' || model_id || '::' || model_version || '::' || quant_tag || '::' || normalize(prefix_text) || '::' || tool_config). TTL set by policy, on access we bump recency. invalidation triggers: model_version change, quant change, explicit admin invalidation, or TTL expiry. eviction logs emit reason codes (TTL, LRU, quota).
[06:42] Lena: note on normalization - strip timestamps, sort JSON keys, canonicalize whitespace, and optionally replace user ids with placeholders; that boosts hit rates.
[06:53] Priya: what's typical hit-rate uplift if we canonicalize?
[06:56] Marco: for our sample we saw canonicalization move 45% -> 60% hit rate; depends on how many tokens are variable metadata.
[07:05] Tom: let's talk storage format - do you persist to disk or keep in GPU memory?
[07:09] Marco: hybrid approach: hot entries in GPU memory for fastest rehydration, warm entries in local NVMe with fast deserialization, cold entries evicted. persistent backing can be S3 for cross-node rehydrate but that adds latency. for Private/on-prem you can configure local SSD tiers.
[07:28] Sara: any extra network exposure if backing is S3?
[07:31] Marco: yes cross-node rehydrate needs network; we recommend keeping hot set local in VPC mode. for hosted we control placement and pre-warm nodes.
[07:41] Priya: concerned about correctness - can stale prefixes cause incorrect outputs?
[07:45] Marco: stale prefixes reflect old system prompt or old instruction state; always make cache keys include explicit versioning for system prompts and use strict invalidation on deploy. as a safety net you can run a lightweight post-check that verifies a checksum of rehydrated prefix matches expected embedding or log-likelihood threshold; if mismatch, fall back to re-evaluate prefix. that costs extra but can prevent regressions.
[08:09] Lena: also runtime supports canarying cache policies - test new TTLs or normalization in a small percent of traffic.
[08:16] Tom: what about debugging - how do we trace a rehydration to a request?
[08:20] Marco: every rehydrate event includes trace id, key fingerprint, node id, and stack; Redwood Console surfaces per-key stats and you can pull the raw rehydrate log. we'll show screenshots in the follow-up docs.
[08:33] Priya: ok this is helpful. any gotchas for on-prem? we run air-gapped in some infra.
[08:39] Lena: on-prem considerations: local KMS/HSM integrations, control-plane connectivity for updates - we provide an on-prem package that runs the control plane in your VPC. cache persistence must be local SSD; cross-node rehydrate can be disabled so all rehydrates are local only. monitoring hooks sent to your local observability stack.
[09:00] Sara: we need to validate that logs don't leak query text - can rehydrate logs be redacted?
[09:05] Marco: yes you can redact or only store hashed fingerprints. we recommend storing full text only in customer-managed encrypted stores.
[09:13] Priya: final question - if we run a pilot, what's the easiest way to measure ROI?
[09:18] Marco: pick a representative route, baseline latency & cost for two weeks without caching, then enable caching and run same load for two weeks. metrics: per-token latency, p95 latency, GPU utilization, tokens-per-dollar. we'll help set that up.
[09:32] Lena: quick recap and next steps - Marco will draft keying strategy doc + TTL recommendations, I'll send SOC2 and the prefix-caching benchmark spreadsheet, Tom will send prompt set and histograms, and we schedule the pilot.
[09:45] Priya: thanks all. Sara - we'll follow-up on security checklist items offline.
[09:50] Sara: thanks, please include redaction options in the docs.
[09:54] Lena: great we'll send notes and set up the pilot ticket. thanks everyone.

End of meeting.
